What This Establishes

Three properties, each one turning "the tree is walkable" from a demo into a structural property:

1. The shim is capability-conditional. test_shim_serves_rooms_for_roomworld, test_shim_404_for_non_roomworld, test_shim_rooms_for_chessworld_404, test_shim_rooms_empty_roomworld — four cases, all driven by the same rule ("has list_rooms() → serve /rooms"). test_shim_regression_other_endpoints — /manifest, /log, /petition, /act still work exactly as before. The change is additive; nothing existing is touched.
2. The default loader works. test_default_loader_works, test_default_loader_empty_roomworld, test_default_loader_returns_none_for_non_roomworld, test_default_loader_unreachable — the loader that C75 defined, and that C75's demo had to bypass with a custom callback, now works against any live RoomWorld. A ChatWorld returns None (no /rooms endpoint), an empty RoomWorld returns [], an unreachable URL returns None. This is the whole gap-closure, and it's verified at the loader level.
3. snapshot_tree works without a callback. test_snapshot_tree_no_callback_single_roomworld, test_snapshot_tree_no_callback_with_children, test_snapshot_tree_deep_nesting, test_snapshot_tree_depth_limits_without_callback — the observation verb now discovers the whole tree, by HTTP, without operator assistance. test_snapshot_tree_custom_loader_still_works — the custom-loader path is unchanged; both styles are valid. test_snapshot_tree_same_result_with_and_without_loader — the two paths produce identical snapshots for the same tree. The loader is optional now, not required.

The honest limits

· /rooms is unauthenticated. Anyone can read a RoomWorld's room list. That is what a directory is: readable by design. A private directory would need a different protocol extension (v0.2).
· /rooms is read-only. Registration is a curator-level operation (RoomWorld.register_room). A v0.2 spec would sign and publish registrations over HTTP.
· public_key in each room entry is unverified. C74 registers it, C76 serves it, but no caller checks the room's manifest against it. A v0.2 spec would verify at register time and at Route time.
· No pagination. A RoomWorld with 10,000 rooms would serve a large JSON blob. Fine for parks and malls; scale is a v0.2 concern.
· _default_room_loader still returns None on network failure. The distinction between "world has no rooms" ([]) and "couldn't reach world" (None) is preserved. snapshot_tree treats both as "no children to walk," which is the right behavior for observation — the walk doesn't fail, it reports what's reachable.

What Was Run

The tests in multiverse_c76_test.py have not been executed against a live Python environment in this session. The expected output derives from the test logic and the behavior of C3's shim, C65's client, C74's RoomWorld, and C75's snapshot_tree. Per the house rule, this is the honest status.

The Series, at C76

The /rooms endpoint closes the last gap in the C74–C76 stack:

Layer Components What it provides
Substrate C1–C52 Identity, transport, worlds, architectures
Propagation C54–C56 Signed relays
Diplomacy C57–C60 Contracts
Ledger C61–C62 Commitment store
Policy C63 Declared rules
Deployment C64–C66 Live federation
Residents C65, C67 Humans + AI
Curators C68–C70 Daemon diplomacy
Room world C73–C74 Worlds containing worlds
Traversable world C75–C76 Walk + observe, by HTTP alone

The user's original framing — "let things happen on their own; create conditions for possibilities to emerge" — is now backed by three structural properties:

· Traversable: any client can walk a tree with enter_path / follow_route.
· Observable: any client can read a tree with snapshot_tree, by HTTP alone.
· No prescribed shape: nothing in C74–C76 says what a tree should look like. The C75 demo's 6-node tree is one operator's choice; the substrate allows any other.

What's next

Two directions remain, and they're genuinely different:

1. C77: The sub-registry route in Route. C75's honest limitation was that Route.target_manifest.act_endpoint is a URI (park://...), not an HTTP URL. C76 made snapshot_tree self-sufficient, but follow_route still needs the caller to supply the room's base_url. A small extension to C74 (have RoomWorld construct the Route's target manifest with act_endpoint=f"{room_base_url}/act") would close this. Then follow_route could work without the caller supplying the URL.
2. C77: The "living tree" spec. A specification — like C61 was — for how a tree grows and dissolves without any central decision. How operators publish a RoomEntry to a parent. How a parent retires. How a client discovers a tree from an arbitrary root URL. How observers can subscribe to a subtree's changes (C56's signed relays applied to room_registered/room_unregistered events). Same discipline as C61: a document, not code.

My instinct: the Route URL extension. It's the smallest piece that closes the last named gap in the C73–C76 stack, and it makes the whole "walk a tree" story client-complete: a client given only a nexus URL can walk to any room in it, following Routes, without ever being told a URL. That's the moment when the tree becomes fully navigable by an outsider, which is exactly the condition the user described. The living-tree spec is the deeper piece, but it can be built on top of a fully navigable tree; the Route extension is what makes navigation complete.

Shall I proceed with C77: The Route URL Extension?


::➡️


Component 77: The Route URL Extension

C75 named the gap: Route.target_manifest.act_endpoint is a URI (park://...), so follow_route needed a caller-supplied base_url. C76 closed half of it — a client can now snapshot_tree by HTTP alone. C77 closes the other half: a client given only a root URL and a chain of room IDs can walk to any room in the tree, because every Route now carries HTTP URLs the client can follow.

The change is small — three edits — and none of them touch the protocol. C74's RoomWorld already knew each room's base_url; C77 makes it use that knowledge when constructing Routes.

Change 1: C75's RouteFollowResult gains a base_url field (additive, default-None)

```python
# In multiverse_c75.py
@dataclass
class RouteFollowResult:
    ok: bool
    verified: bool
    world_id: str
    reason: str
    admission_raw: Optional[Dict] = None
    base_url: Optional[str] = None   # NEW: where the client ended up
```

_enter_at_url sets it (base_url=base on both the success and the fail path). Existing callers unaffected.

Change 2: C77's resolve_manifest_urls — the URL substitution

```python
def resolve_manifest_urls(
    manifest: Manifest, base_url: str,
) -> Manifest:
    """Return a copy of manifest with non-HTTP endpoint URIs
    resolved to HTTP URLs rooted at base_url.

    A RoomWorld knows each room's HTTP base URL. Its declared
    manifest may still carry URI-scheme endpoints
    (`park://.../act`). The Route the RoomWorld returns is a
    *pointer* to the room — it is legitimate (and useful) for
    the pointer to carry HTTP URLs, even though the room's
    published manifest has URIs. This helper does that
    substitution.
    """
    base = base_url.rstrip("/")
    def resolve(uri: str, path: str) -> str:
        if uri.startswith(("http://", "https://")):
            return uri
        return f"{base}/{path}"
    return replace(
        manifest,
        law_url=resolve(manifest.law_url, "law"),
        act_endpoint=resolve(manifest.act_endpoint, "act"),
        log_endpoint=resolve(manifest.log_endpoint, "log"),
    )
```

Change 3: C77's UrlResolvingRoomWorld — the RoomWorld that resolves

```python
class UrlResolvingRoomWorld(RoomWorld):
    """A RoomWorld whose Routes carry HTTP URLs.

    Subclasses C74's RoomWorld; overrides only _route_to_room.
    C74's RoomWorld is unchanged, and its Routes still carry
    the room's declared URI endpoints. Deployments that want
    URL-followable Routes use this class instead.
    """

    def _route_to_room(self, petition):
        # Same logic as C74._route_to_room, but the returned
        # Route's target_manifest has its URIs resolved.
        result = super()._route_to_room(petition)
        if not isinstance(result, Route):
            return result
        entry = next(
            (r for r in self.list_rooms()
             if r["room_id"] == petition.target), None)
        if entry is None:
            return result
        return Route(
            target_manifest=resolve_manifest_urls(
                result.target_manifest, entry["base_url"]),
            reason=result.reason,
        )
```

multiverse_c77.py — the walker, at last self-sufficient

```python
"""
multiverse_c77.py — Component 77: The Route URL Extension.

Closes C75's last gap. Before C77, walking a tree required
the caller to know each room's HTTP base URL. After C77:

  - UrlResolvingRoomWorld builds Routes whose
    target_manifest endpoints are HTTP URLs.
  - follow_route can derive base_url from the Route itself
    (backward-compatible: caller-supplied base_url still wins).
  - walk_to(client, root_url, path) walks a chain of room
    ids from any root URL, needing nothing else.

The nested C74/C75/C76 worlds are unchanged; only Route
construction and follow_route's defaults differ. The client
is now self-sufficient against any tree whose parents use
UrlResolvingRoomWorld.

Composition: C3 (Manifest, Route), C74 (RoomWorld), C75
(follow_route, snapshot_tree), C76 (/rooms endpoint). No
new artifacts, no protocol change.

Honest limits (documented, tested):
  - A Route from a plain C74 RoomWorld still needs a
    caller-supplied base_url. C77 doesn't retrofit C74 —
    it provides a subclass. Deployments choose.
  - URL substitution happens per-Route, not on the
    published manifest. GET /manifest still returns
    URI-scheme endpoints for a UrlResolvingRoomWorld.
    That's correct: the world *is* located at a URI;
    the Route is a pointer to its HTTP location.
  - walk_to assumes the root world admits on first
    petition (as C74 worlds do). A world with a stricter
    Law would refuse, and walk_to would stop there.
  - walk_to uses raw HTTP against each world's /petition,
    not C65's anchor-anchored client, because the target
    worlds may not be in the client's anchors. Verifying
    each hop's admission is the caller's job (via
    expected_public_key when they know the key).
"""

from dataclasses import replace
from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional

from multiverse_c3 import Manifest, Petition, Route, Act, Ack, Refusal
from multiverse_c65 import FederationClient
from multiverse_c74 import RoomWorld, RoomEntry
from multiverse_c75 import (
    RouteFollowResult, _enter_at_url, _http_post, _HTTPError,
    follow_route as _follow_route_c75,
)


# =====================================================================
# resolve_manifest_urls
# =====================================================================

def resolve_manifest_urls(
    manifest: Manifest, base_url: str,
) -> Manifest:
    base = base_url.rstrip("/")
    def resolve(uri: str, path: str) -> str:
        if uri.startswith(("http://", "https://")):
            return uri
        return f"{base}/{path}"
    return replace(
        manifest,
        law_url=resolve(manifest.law_url, "law"),
        act_endpoint=resolve(manifest.act_endpoint, "act"),
        log_endpoint=resolve(manifest.log_endpoint, "log"),
    )


# =====================================================================
# UrlResolvingRoomWorld
# =====================================================================

class UrlResolvingRoomWorld(RoomWorld):
    """A RoomWorld whose Routes carry HTTP URLs."""

    def _route_to_room(self, petition: Petition):
        result = super()._route_to_room(petition)
        if not isinstance(result, Route):
            return result
        entry = next(
            (r for r in self.list_rooms()
             if r["room_id"] == petition.target), None)
        if entry is None:
            return result
        return Route(
            target_manifest=resolve_manifest_urls(
                result.target_manifest, entry["base_url"]),
            reason=result.reason,
        )


# =====================================================================
# follow_route — optional base_url, derived from Route
# =====================================================================

def follow_route(
    client: FederationClient,
    route: Route,
    room_base_url: Optional[str] = None,
    expected_public_key: Optional[str] = None,
) -> RouteFollowResult:
    """C77 supersedes C75's follow_route: `room_base_url` is
    now optional. If omitted, it is derived from
    route.target_manifest.act_endpoint.

    Backward compatible: callers that pass room_base_url
    positionally (C75's signature) still work.
    """
    if not isinstance(route, Route):
        return RouteFollowResult(
            False, False, "", "not a Route")
    if room_base_url is None:
        uri = route.target_manifest.act_endpoint
        if not uri.startswith(("http://", "https://")):
            return RouteFollowResult(
                False, False, route.target_manifest.entity_id,
                ("route has no HTTP URL; caller must supply "
                 "room_base_url (this Route may come from a "
                 "plain C74 RoomWorld, not a UrlResolving "
                 "one)"))
        room_base_url = uri[:-len("/act")] if uri.endswith("/act") else uri
    return _enter_at_url(
        client,
        base_url=room_base_url,
        expected_public_key=expected_public_key,
        label=route.target_manifest.entity_id,
    )


# =====================================================================
# walk_to — the payoff
# =====================================================================

def walk_to(
    client: FederationClient,
    root_url: str,
    path: List[str],
    expected_public_key: Optional[str] = None,
) -> List[RouteFollowResult]:
    """Walk from root_url through a chain of room IDs.

    The client is given:
      - the root's HTTP URL,
      - a list of room IDs (as they appear in each parent's
        /rooms listing or register_room call),
      - optionally a public key to verify each hop.

    The client is NOT given:
      - intermediate rooms' URLs,
      - their manifests,
      - their public keys.

    walk_to uses the Route each parent returns to discover the
    next URL. If every parent is a UrlResolvingRoomWorld, no
    caller-supplied URL is needed past the root.

    Returns a list of RouteFollowResults — one for the root
    entry, one per room entered. Stops on first failure.
    """
    results: List[RouteFollowResult] = []

    # 1. Enter the root
    r = _enter_at_url(
        client, base_url=root_url,
        expected_public_key=expected_public_key,
        label=root_url)
    results.append(r)
    if not r.ok:
        return results
    current_url = r.base_url or root_url

    # 2. Walk the path
    for room_id in path:
        try:
            resp = _http_post(f"{current_url}/petition", {
                "petitioner_token":
                    client.state.identity.identity.token,
                "petitioner_name":
                    client.state.identity.identity.name,
                "passport_admissions": list(
                    client.state.passport.to_plain_entries()),
                "message": "walk",
                "target": room_id,
            })
        except _HTTPError as e:
            results.append(RouteFollowResult(
                False, False, room_id,
                f"petition failed: {e}"))
            return results
        if resp.get("kind") != "route":
            results.append(RouteFollowResult(
                False, False, room_id,
                f"expected route, got {resp.get('kind')!r}: "
                f"{resp.get('reason', '')}"))
            return results
        try:
            m = resp["target_manifest"]
            target_manifest = Manifest(
                entity_id=m["entity_id"],
                name=m["name"],
                protocol_version=m["protocol_version"],
                law_url=m["law_url"],
                act_endpoint=m["act_endpoint"],
                log_endpoint=m["log_endpoint"],
                sub_registry_endpoint=m.get(
                    "sub_registry_endpoint"))
        except (KeyError, TypeError) as e:
            results.append(RouteFollowResult(
                False, False, room_id,
                f"malformed route manifest: {e}"))
            return results
        route = Route(
            target_manifest=target_manifest,
            reason=resp.get("reason", ""))
        fr = follow_route(
            client, route,
            expected_public_key=expected_public_key)
        results.append(fr)
        if not fr.ok:
            return results
        if fr.base_url is None:
            results.append(RouteFollowResult(
                False, False, room_id,
                "follow_route returned no base_url"))
            return results
        current_url = fr.base_url

    return results
```

Demo — the payoff

```python
def demo(artifact_dir: Optional[str] = None) -> Dict:
    """Walk the tree from the nexus URL alone.

    The client is given:
      - world:nexus's URL,
      - the path ["world:games", "world:chess"].

    It is NOT given the URLs of world:games or world:chess.
    It discovers both from the Route each parent returns.
    """
    import json as _json
    import time
    from pathlib import Path
    from multiverse_c1 import create_identity
    from multiverse_c13 import HAS_CRYPTO
    from multiverse_c73 import ChessWorld, HAS_CHESS
    from multiverse_c74 import RoomEntry
    from multiverse_c75 import _http_post
    from wcp_http_shim import WorldProtocolServer

    if not HAS_CRYPTO:
        raise RuntimeError("demo requires `cryptography`")
    if not HAS_CHESS:
        raise RuntimeError(
            "demo requires `python-chess` (pip install chess)")

    if artifact_dir is None:
        artifact_dir = "artifacts"
    path = Path(artifact_dir) / "route_urls"
    path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    # Build a UrlResolvingRoomWorld tree
    chess = ChessWorld("world:chess", "Chess Table")
    plaza = ChatWorld("world:plaza", "Plaza")
    games = UrlResolvingRoomWorld("world:games", "Games Hall")
    nexus = UrlResolvingRoomWorld("world:nexus", "The Nexus")

    servers = {}
    urls = {}
    for world, wname in (
        (chess, "chess"), (plaza, "plaza"),
        (games, "games"), (nexus, "nexus"),
    ):
        srv = WorldProtocolServer(world, port=0)
        srv.serve_in_thread()
        servers[wname] = srv
        urls[wname] = (
            f"http://127.0.0.1:"
            f"{srv._httpd.server_address[1]}")
    time.sleep(0.2)

    games.register_room(RoomEntry(
        parent_world_id="world:games",
        room_id="world:chess",
        base_url=urls["chess"],
        public_key="00" * 32,
        name="Chess Table"))
    games.register_room(RoomEntry(
        parent_world_id="world:games",
        room_id="world:plaza",
        base_url=urls["plaza"],
        public_key="00" * 32,
        name="Games Plaza"))
    nexus.register_room(RoomEntry(
        parent_world_id="world:nexus",
        room_id="world:games",
        base_url=urls["games"],
        public_key="00" * 32,
        name="Games Hall"))

    try:
        client_dir = path / "alice"
        if client_dir.exists():
            import shutil
            shutil.rmtree(client_dir)
        client = FederationClient(client_dir)
        client.create_identity("Alice")

        # The client knows ONLY the nexus URL and the path.
        # It does NOT know world:games's URL or world:chess's URL.
        walk = walk_to(
            client,
            root_url=urls["nexus"],
            path=["world:games", "world:chess"],
        )

        # If we made it, sit at chess. We get chess's URL from
        # the last walk result — but the walk itself never needed
        # to know it.
        chess_url_from_walk = walk[-1].base_url if walk[-1].ok else None
        if chess_url_from_walk is not None:
            _http_post(f"{chess_url_from_walk}/act", {
                "actor_token":
                    client.state.identity.identity.token,
                "type": "chess.sit",
                "payload": {"seat": "white"},
            })

        # Print
        print("=" * 70)
        print("Route URL Extension — the tree, walked by URL alone")
        print("=" * 70)
        print()
        print(f"  Nexus URL (the only URL given): {urls['nexus']}")
        print(f"  Requested path: {['world:games', 'world:chess']}")
        print()
        print(f"  Intermediate URLs the client did NOT know:")
        print(f"    world:games  at  {urls['games']}")
        print(f"    world:chess  at  {urls['chess']}")
        print()
        print("  The walk:")
        for r in walk:
            marker = "✓" if (r.ok and r.verified) else (
                "○" if r.ok else "✗")
            base = r.base_url or "(no url)"
            print(f"    {marker} {r.world_id}")
            print(f"        entered at {base}")
            print(f"        {r.reason}")
        print()
        print(f"  Passport entries: {len(client.state.passport)}")
        print()
        print("  What this demonstrates:")
        print("    - A UrlResolvingRoomWorld returns Routes whose")
        print("      target manifests carry HTTP URLs. The room's")
        print("      own published manifest keeps its URI-scheme")
        print("      endpoints — the Route is a pointer that")
        print("      resolves them.")
        print("    - follow_route's base_url parameter is now")
        print("      optional. When omitted, it derives from the")
        print("      Route. Backward compatible.")
        print("    - walk_to(client, nexus_url, [games, chess])")
        print("      reaches a leaf without any external URL")
        print("      knowledge. The tree is fully navigable by a")
        print("      client that knows only the root.")
        print()
        print("  Anchor (public domain, Emily Dickinson):")
        print("    'I dwell in Possibility –'")
        print("    'A fairer House than Prose –'")
        print("    'More numerous of Windows –'")
        print("    'Superior – for Doors –'")

        audit = {
            "nexus_url": urls["nexus"],
            "hidden_urls": {
                "world:games": urls["games"],
                "world:chess": urls["chess"],
            },
            "walk": [
                {"world_id": r.world_id, "ok": r.ok,
                 "verified": r.verified,
                 "base_url": r.base_url, "reason": r.reason}
                for r in walk
            ],
            "passport_entries": len(client.state.passport),
            "reached_chess": (
                walk and walk[-1].ok
                and walk[-1].world_id == "world:chess"),
        }
        (path / "route_urls_demo.json").write_text(
            _json.dumps(audit, indent=2))
        print(f"\n  → {path}/route_urls_demo.json")
        return audit
    finally:
        for srv in servers.values():
            srv.stop()
```

```python
import json

    reason="cryptography and/or python-chess not installed")


def _serve(world):
    srv = WorldProtocolServer(world, port=0)
    srv.serve_in_thread()
    time.sleep(0.1)
    return srv, f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv._httpd.server_address[1]}"


def _client(tmp_path, name="Alice"):
    c = FederationClient(tmp_path / "c")
    c.create_identity(name)
    return c


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# resolve_manifest_urls

def test_resolve_substitutes_uri_endpoints():
    print("=== resolve_manifest_urls: URI → HTTP ===")
    m = Manifest(
        entity_id="w", name="W", protocol_version="WCP/0.2",
        law_url="park://w/law",
        act_endpoint="park://w/act",
        log_endpoint="park://w/log",
        sub_registry_endpoint=None)
    resolved = resolve_manifest_urls(m, "http://host:1234")
    assert resolved.law_url == "http://host:1234/law"
    assert resolved.act_endpoint == "http://host:1234/act"
    assert resolved.log_endpoint == "http://host:1234/log"
    # entity_id, name unchanged
    assert resolved.entity_id == "w"
    # original untouched
    assert m.act_endpoint == "park://w/act"


def test_resolve_preserves_http_endpoints():
    print("=== resolve_manifest_urls: existing HTTP preserved ===")
    m = Manifest(
        entity_id="w", name="W", protocol_version="WCP/0.2",
        law_url="https://other/law",
        act_endpoint="https://other/act",
        log_endpoint="https://other/log",
        sub_registry_endpoint=None)
    resolved = resolve_manifest_urls(m, "http://host:1234")
    assert resolved.law_url == "https://other/law"
    assert resolved.act_endpoint == "https://other/act"

# UrlResolvingRoomWorld
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_url_resolving_roomworld_route_has_http_urls():
    print("=== UrlResolvingRoomWorld: Route has HTTP URLs ===")
    inner = ChatWorld("world:inner", "Inner")
    s1, u1 = _serve(inner)
    games = UrlResolvingRoomWorld("world:games", "Games")
    s2, u2 = _serve(games)
    try:
        games.register_room(RoomEntry(
            parent_world_id="world:games",
            room_id="world:inner", base_url=u1,
            public_key="00" * 32, name="Inner"))
        alice = create_identity("Alice")
        games.petition(Petition(
            petitioner_token=alice.token,
            petitioner_name=alice.name,
            passport_admissions=(), message=""))
        route = games.petition(Petition(
            petitioner_token=alice.token,
            petitioner_name=alice.name,
            passport_admissions=(), message="",
            target="world:inner"))
        assert isinstance(route, Route)
        # The target manifest has HTTP URLs
        assert route.target_manifest.act_endpoint.startswith(
            u1.rstrip("/") + "/act")
        assert route.target_manifest.log_endpoint.startswith(
            u1.rstrip("/") + "/log")
        # Its declared (published) manifest still has URI scheme
        assert inner.manifest().act_endpoint.startswith("chat://")
    finally:
        s1.stop()
        s2.stop()

def test_follow_route_fails_with_uri_only_route(tmp_path):
    print("=== follow_route: URI-only Route → fail ===")
    inner = ChatWorld("world:inner", "Inner")
    games = RoomWorld("world:games", "Games")
    alice = create_identity("Alice")
    games.petition(Petition(
        petitioner_token=alice.token,
        petitioner_name=alice.name,
        passport_admissions=(), message=""))
    games.register_room(RoomEntry(
        parent_world_id="world:games",
        room_id="world:inner", base_url="http://example",
        public_key="00" * 32, name="Inner"))
    # NOTE: we can't actually serve the inner world for this test,
    # but the Route is constructed from the declared (URI) manifest
    route = games.petition(Petition(
        petitioner_token=alice.token,
        petitioner_name=alice.name,
        passport_admissions=(), message="",
        target="world:inner"))
    # Try to follow without base_url — should fail with a clear
    # message about needing base_url
    c = _client(tmp_path)
    # But the URI route can't be followed without a URL. This
    # exercises follow_route's URI guard.
    from multiverse_c77 import follow_route as c77_follow
    # Force a URI-only Route by using RoomWorld's declared manifest
    # (still URI scheme)
    from multiverse_c3 import Route as R
    uri_route = R(
        target_manifest=inner.manifest(),
        reason="test")
    r = c77_follow(c, uri_route)
    assert not r.ok
    assert "room_base_url" in r.reason or "HTTP URL" in r.reason


def test_follow_route_with_explicit_base_url_still_works(tmp_path):
    print("=== follow_route: explicit base_url (C75 compat) ===")
    inner = ChatWorld("world:inner", "Inner")

# walk_to

def test_walk_to_full_chain(tmp_path):
    print("=== walk_to: full chain, URL-only ===")
    inner = ChatWorld("world:inner", "Inner")
    middle = UrlResolvingRoomWorld("world:mid", "Mid")
    outer = UrlResolvingRoomWorld("world:out", "Out")
    s1, u1 = _serve(inner)
    s2, u2 = _serve(middle)
    s3, u3 = _serve(outer)
    try:
        middle.register_room(RoomEntry(
            parent_world_id="world:mid",
            room_id="world:inner", base_url=u1,
            public_key="00" * 32, name="Inner"))
        outer.register_room(RoomEntry(
            parent_world_id="world:out",
            room_id="world:mid", base_url=u2,
            public_key="00" * 32, name="Mid"))
        c = _client(tmp_path)
        # Client knows ONLY u3 (the root URL) and the path.
        walk = walk_to(c, u3, ["world:mid", "world:inner"])
        assert all(r.ok for r in walk), [r.reason for r in walk]
        assert len(walk) == 3  # root + 2 rooms
        assert walk[0].world_id == "world:out"
        assert walk[1].world_id == "world:mid"
        assert walk[2].world_id == "world:inner"
        assert len(c.state.passport) == 3
    finally:
        s1.stop()
        s2.stop()
        s3.stop()


def test_walk_to_stops_on_failure(tmp_path):
    print("=== walk_to: stops on unreachable room ===")
    outer = UrlResolvingRoomWorld("world:out", "Out")
    s3, u3 = _serve(outer)
    try:
        outer.register_room(RoomEntry(
            parent_world_id="world:out",
            room_id="world:gone", base_url="http://127.0.0.1:1",
            public_key="00" * 32, name="Gone"))
        c = _client(tmp_path)
        walk = walk_to(c, u3, ["world:gone"])
        # root ok, room fail
        assert walk[0].ok
        assert not walk[-1].ok
    finally:
        s3.stop()


def test_walk_to_unknown_room(tmp_path):
    print("=== walk_to: unknown room → stop ===")
    outer = UrlResolvingRoomWorld("world:out", "Out")
    s3, u3 = _serve(outer)
    try:
        c = _client(tmp_path)
        walk = walk_to(c, u3, ["world:nonexistent"])
        assert walk[0].ok
        assert not walk[-1].ok
        assert "expected route" in walk[-1].reason.lower() \
            or "unknown" in walk[-1].reason.lower()
    finally:
        s3.stop()


def test_walk_to_empty_path(tmp_path):
    print("=== walk_to: empty path → just root ===")
    outer = UrlResolvingRoomWorld("world:out", "Out")
    s3, u3 = _serve(outer)
    try:
        c = _client(tmp_path)
        walk = walk_to(c, u3, [])
        assert len(walk) == 1
        assert walk[0].ok
    finally:
        s3.stop()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demo
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_demo(tmp_path):
    print("=== Demo: walk tree by URL alone ===")
    audit = demo(artifact_dir=str(tmp_path))
    assert audit["reached_chess"] is True
    assert len(audit["walk"]) == 3
    assert all(r["ok"] for r in audit["walk"])
    # The client never saw the intermediate URLs
    assert audit["hidden_urls"]["world:games"] != audit["nexus_url"]
    assert audit["hidden_urls"]["world:chess"] != audit["nexus_url"]
    # But the walk results expose them
    assert audit["walk"][1]["base_url"] == audit["hidden_urls"]["world:games"]
    assert audit["walk"][2]["base_url"] == audit["hidden_urls"]["world:chess"]
```

What This Establishes

Four properties, each one closing the walk-a-tree story in the way the user framed it:

1. The Route is now a real pointer. test_url_resolving_roomworld_route_has_http_urls — a UrlResolvingRoomWorld returns Routes with HTTP endpoints. test_plain_roomworld_route_has_uris — a plain C74 RoomWorld still returns URI-scheme Routes; both behaviors coexist. test_resolve_substitutes_uri_endpoints and test_resolve_preserves_http_endpoints — the substitution is only for URIs, HTTP endpoints pass through untouched. The published manifest is unchanged.
2. follow_route self-sufficient against C77 worlds, still C75-compatible. test_follow_route_derives_base_url — given only a Route from a UrlResolvingRoomWorld, follow_route enters the target. test_follow_route_with_explicit_base_url_still_works — C75's signature still works. test_follow_route_fails_with_uri_only_route — a Route from a plain C74 world fails cleanly with a reason that names the missing input, rather than guessing.
3. walk_to is the payoff. test_walk_to_full_chain — a client given only the root URL and a path of room IDs reaches the leaf. test_walk_to_stops_on_failure, test_walk_to_unknown_room — the walk halts at the first failure with a clear reason and a complete trace up to that point. test_walk_to_empty_path — a degenerate case (just enter the root) works.
4. The demo makes the narrative concrete. test_demo asserts:
   · reached_chess is true,
   · the intermediate URLs are distinct from the root URL (so "the client didn't know them" is a real claim),
   · the walk results do expose the intermediate URLs (the client learned them, but only from the Route).
   That's the story: the tree is fully navigable by a client that only knows the root — and that navigability is a property of the Route's content, not of any client-side secret or prior knowledge.

The honest limits

· C74's RoomWorld unchanged. A Route from a plain RoomWorld still needs caller-supplied base_url. UrlResolvingRoomWorld is a subclass; deployments choose. test_follow_route_fails_with_uri_only_route shows what happens when a Route from a plain world is followed without a URL.
· Route vs manifest are different artifacts. A UrlResolvingRoomWorld's GET /manifest still returns URI endpoints — because it is at a URI. The Route is a pointer to an HTTP location. test_url_resolving_roomworld_route_has_http_urls verifies both facts in one test.
· walk_to uses raw HTTP, not C65's anchored client. If the caller wants each hop's admission verified, they pass expected_public_key (used at every hop). Otherwise, admissions are recorded but unverified (visible in RouteFollowResult.verified). This is the honest default — a stranger should be able to walk without knowing every room's key, but should not be lied to about verification status.
· walk_to is single-path, no branching. It follows one chain of room IDs. A caller who wants to explore the tree first uses snapshot_tree; then walk_to. Two verbs, two purposes.

What Was Run

The tests in multiverse_c77_test.py have not been executed against a live Python environment in this session. The expected output derives from the test logic and the behavior of C3's Route, C74's RoomWorld, C75's follow_route, C76's /rooms endpoint. Per the house rule, this is the honest status.

The Series, at C77

The room-world stack is now client-complete:

Component What it provides
C73 Chess park (a real room type)
C74 RoomWorld (a world that is a directory)
C75 Follow/observe verbs (follow_route, snapshot_tree)
C76 /rooms endpoint (self-sufficient observation)
C77 URL-resolving Routes (self-sufficient traversal)

The traversal story is now: a client that knows only a root URL can discover and reach any room in the tree, by HTTP alone, using only the protocol's existing petition + Route + manifest operations. No client-side secret. No caller-supplied intermediate URLs. No assumption about the tree's shape.

That's the user's framing made literal: conditions for possibilities to emerge. The substrate provides traversal (C77), observation (C76), and no shape rules. Trees can form, dissolve, nest, and cross as operators choose. What patterns appear is emergent — the components just make them reachable.

What's next

Two directions remain, and they're at different scopes:

1. C78: The living-tree spec. A specification (like C61) for how trees change over time — how a RoomEntry is published and verified by a parent (a room_register signed artifact), how a parent signals a room's retirement (a room_closed event), how an observer subscribes to a subtree's structural events via signed relays (C56). Same discipline: a document, not code. C74–C77 established what a tree is; C78 would be what a tree does over time.
2. C78: The demonstration runner, extended. C71 has 26 demos across 9 layers. C72–C77 add seven more (inter-federation, chess, room world, traversable, /rooms, route URLs). A make arc that runs all of them and produces a single comparative summary would be the definitive single-command arc. Packaging.

My instinct: the living-tree spec. The user's framing — "create conditions for possibilities to emerge" — has always been about process, not structure. C74–C77 establish static structure (a room-world is a directory) and the conditions for using it (traversable, observable). What's missing is the temporal dimension: how a tree can grow, dissolve, and evolve without anyone prescribing its shape. That's what a specification — a discipline of how changes are published and verified — can provide, without ever dictating what changes should happen.

The arc has demonstrated that structure can emerge from operator choices. The living-tree spec would formalize the discipline that keeps that emergence legible and verifiable over time. That's the natural completion of the room-world line.

Shall I proceed with C78: The Living Tree Spec?


::➡️


Component 78: The Living Tree Spec

C74–C77 built a tree you can walk and see. C78 is the discipline that keeps the tree legible while it changes. It is a specification — not code, following the pattern of C61 (the ledger spec) and C64 (the deployment spec). The document itself is the artifact.

---

LTS/0.1 — The Living Tree Specification

A discipline for how worlds are added to, retired from, and observed within a tree of rooms, without any central authority deciding what the tree should look like.

---

1. Purpose

C74 defined a RoomWorld — a world that is a directory of rooms. C75 gave clients verbs to walk a tree and read it. C76 made /rooms self-sufficient over HTTP. C77 made Routes HTTP-followable so a client with just a root URL can reach any room.

All of that gives the tree a shape. None of it gives the tree a history.

A park at noon is not the same park at midnight. Rooms open and close; tenants rotate; a chess table becomes a poetry reading; a hall that hosted three rooms hosts two. LTS is the discipline for how those changes are published and verified over time, such that any client joining the tree later can reconstruct its current state and its relevant history without ever having been present when the changes happened.

The spec's core claim: a tree can change without anyone prescribing its shape, and any observer can verify that the changes were legitimate.

That's a stronger claim than C74–C77 make. C74–C77 say "the tree is what it is." LTS says "the tree is what its signed history says it is."

2. What "Living" Means

A tree is living when it satisfies three properties:

1. Each change is a signed artifact. A room entering the tree, a room leaving the tree, a room's URL being updated, a room's public_key being rotated — each is a RoomLifecycleEvent, signed by an authority whose claim is verifiable against the parent's Law.
2. Each change is verifiable independently. A third party can check any lifecycle event without contacting the parent (except once, to fetch the parent's current manifest), and can reconstruct any historical state from the sequence of events.
3. No authority decides the tree's shape. The parent's Law says what kinds of lifecycle events are valid. It does not say what the tree should be. The tree emerges from the events operators publish.

A tree that fails (1) is a black box — you see the current state but not how it got there.
A tree that fails (2) is unverifiable — you must trust whoever's telling you.
A tree that fails (3) is a platform — the shape is designed, not grown.

All three must hold for the tree to be called living.

3. The Problem the Spec Solves

C74–C77 have three known gaps in the temporal dimension:

Gap 1: unregistered ≠ retired. C74's unregister_room removes a room from the directory. But there's no distinction between "the operator retired this room" and "the room was never there." An observer joining later sees a parent with one fewer room and cannot tell whether a retirement happened. This is the same problem C59/C60 solved at the federation level; LTS solves it at the tree level.

Gap 2: no subscription. A client cannot say "tell me when rooms are added or removed from this subtree." They have to poll /rooms and diff. That's workable but not the same as subscribing — and it means no client can serve as an observer that publishes what it saw to others.

Gap 3: no chained verification for historical states. If Alice walked the tree yesterday and Carol walks it today, there's no way for Carol to check "the tree I see today is a legitimate descendant of the tree Alice saw." She can verify today's state (against today's rooms' signatures), but she cannot verify continuity.

LTS defines the artifacts and protocol that close these three gaps.

4. What a Tree Is (recap)

A tree is a rooted directed graph where:

· Each node is a WCP world (C3), identified by its entity_id.
· Each node may or may not have a sub_registry_endpoint in its manifest.
· Each node with a sub-registry lists zero or more rooms, each of which is a {room_id, base_url, public_key, name, description} (C74's RoomEntry).
· Each room is itself a node in the tree.

LTS does not change any of the above. It adds artifacts that change the directory over time, and a protocol that makes those changes verifiable.

5. The Artifact Types

LTS adds three new artifact kinds. All use C13's Ed25519 signatures. All use the canonical_bytes/sign/verify pattern already established in the arc.

5.1 RoomLifecycleEvent

The atomic unit. A signed statement that a room's membership in the tree changed.

```
{
  "kind": "room_lifecycle_event",
  "event_type": "registered" | "retired" | "updated",
  "parent_id": "<parent's entity_id>",
  "room_id": "<room's entity_id>",
  "room_url": "<http(s) base URL>",
  "room_public_key": "<64 hex>",
  "room_name": "<display name>",
  "room_description": "<optional>",
  "prior_event_hash": "<64 hex or null>",
  "timestamp": "<ISO 8601>",
  "signer_id": "<parent's curator world_id>",
  "signer_public_key": "<64 hex>",
  "signature": "<128 hex>"
}
```

Fields:

· event_type — registered (room added), retired (room removed), updated (one of name/url/key changed; the other fields stay as before).
· parent_id — the entity_id of the world whose directory this event changes.
· room_id, room_url, room_public_key, room_name, room_description — the room's post-event state. For retired, only room_id and event_type are meaningful; the others are ignored.
· prior_event_hash — the hash of the immediately-preceding RoomLifecycleEvent for the same (parent_id, room_id) pair, or null if this is the first event. This chains each room's lifecycle events, so tampering with any historical event breaks the chain from that point forward.
· signer_id, signer_public_key, signature — the parent's curator signs the event. This is the same (curator, root_key) relationship as C55's CuratorMessage. A parent is not allowed to sign with an arbitrary key; only its declared curator key.
· timestamp — a claim, not a verified fact. See §9.

5.2 TreeSubscription

A client's claim that it wants to know about structural changes in a subtree.

```
{
  "kind": "tree_subscription",
  "subscriber_id": "<client's entity_id>",
  "subscriber_public_key": "<64 hex>",
  "root_id": "<the subtree's root entity_id>",
  "root_url": "<http(s) base URL>",
  "depth": <integer, max 8>,
  "callback_url": "<http(s) URL the subscriber will accept events at>",
  "since_event_hash": "<64 hex or null>",
  "timestamp": "<ISO 8601>",
  "signer_id": "<subscriber's curator world_id>",
  "signer_public_key": "<64 hex>",
  "signature": "<128 hex>"
}
```

A subscription is itself a signed artifact. The subscriber agrees to accept POSTed TreeEventNotification messages at callback_url. The root (or any intermediary) delivers them per C56's signed-relay discipline.

depth limits the subscription to N levels of the subtree. since_event_hash lets a subscriber resume from a known point.

5.3 TreeEventNotification

A RoomLifecycleEvent delivered to a subscriber.

```
{
  "kind": "tree_event_notification",
  "subscription_hash": "<hash of the TreeSubscription>",
  "event": <a RoomLifecycleEvent>,
  "delivered_at": "<ISO 8601>",
  "relay_chain": [
    {"relayer_id": "...", "relayer_public_key": "...",
     "received_at": "...", "signature": "..."},
    ...
  ]
}
```

The relay_chain is C56's signed relay applied to tree events: each hop that forwarded the event signs that it saw and forwarded it. A subscriber can verify the chain from the original signer (the parent) through every relayer to itself.

6. The Lifecycle of a Room

Each room in a tree has a lifecycle. LTS formalizes it:

A. Registration. A room enters the tree when its parent signs a RoomLifecycleEvent with event_type="registered". The event's prior_event_hash is null (first appearance) or the hash of the last retirement (re-registration).

B. Updates. A room's name, URL, or public_key can change. Each change is a RoomLifecycleEvent with event_type="updated", prior_event_hash chained to the previous event. The room stays present throughout.

C. Retirement. A room leaves the tree when its parent signs a RoomLifecycleEvent with event_type="retired". prior_event_hash chains to the last event. Only room_id matters; other fields are ignored.

D. Re-registration. A retired room can re-enter the tree via a new registered event with prior_event_hash chained to the retirement. This is distinguished from "the room was never there" — the chain says it was retired and has now returned.

E. No forced retirement. A parent's Law decides under what conditions it may retire a room. LTS doesn't prescribe this. A parent might require advance notice; another might retire freely; another might never retire. The protocol is the same; the policy is local.

The room's published history is the chain of events, ordered by prior_event_hash, ending at the current event. Any observer with the chain can reconstruct any historical state.

7. Subscription and Observation

LTS formalizes two observer roles.

A. The passive observer. A client that walks the tree (C75 snapshot_tree) and reads whatever /rooms returns. This is unsubscribed observation. It sees the tree's current state, not its history. It is legitimate for a client that wants to use the tree (find a chess game, read a poem).

B. The subscribed observer. A client that registers a TreeSubscription and receives TreeEventNotifications. This is subscribed observation. It sees every change from the moment of subscription, and can reconstruct history from the events it has received plus whatever the tree serves on /rooms at subscription time.

The distinction matters because:

· A passive observer is right now but has no history. If it wants to check "did the tree change since I last looked?", it must remember what it saw and diff.
· A subscribed observer has history but must maintain state. It is the natural producer of a TreeEventNotification for others — it can subscribe to many subtrees and relay changes to its own subscribers.

This makes a web of subscriptions possible, with each node in the web a signed relay. A client that trusts one trusted observer inherits that observer's whole coverage of the tree.

8. Verification Rules

An observer verifying a RoomLifecycleEvent follows these steps:

1. Reconstruct the canonical payload. The payload is the RoomLifecycleEvent minus the signature field.
2. Resolve the parent's curator key. Either the observer knows it (from curator_public_key in the parent's anchors) or fetches the parent's manifest and reads signed_by/public_key.
3. Verify the signature against the parent's curator key. If it fails, the event is invalid — no downstream check matters.
4. If prior_event_hash is non-null, verify the chain. The observer must have (or be able to fetch) the prior event, whose hash must match. This is what makes historical states verifiable.
5. If a relay_chain is present, verify each hop. Each relayer's signature is checked against its declared key; each hop must have received the event before it forwarded it (per the timestamps, not the actual claim — see §9).

Steps 1–3 are required for any event. Steps 4–5 are required only if the observer cares about continuity or provenance, which a subscribed observer does and a passive observer may not.

TreeSubscription and TreeEventNotification are verified the same way, against the subscriber's and relayer's declared public keys.

9. Timestamps and Time

LTS does not define a global clock. Every artifact's timestamp is a claim, signed by its author. The spec's claim of order comes from prior_event_hash chains, not from timestamps.

That means:

· Two RoomLifecycleEvents for the same room whose timestamps disagree but whose chains agree are ordered by the chain, not by the timestamps.
· A retired event and a registered event that arrive out of order can be re-ordered by chain reconstruction. The client's job is to reconstruct the chain; the parent's job is only to sign the events in the order it emitted them.

For continuity checks between two observers (Alice walked the tree yesterday, Carol walks it today), the chain is the continuity. Alice's final event hash is a claim about which state she saw. Carol can check "is my last event a descendant of Alice's final event?" — if yes, the tree she sees is a descendant of the tree Alice saw. If no, one of them has seen a fork, and LTS does not resolve forks; that's a §11 concern.

10. Composition with Existing Components

LTS adds no primitives and changes no other component.

· C13 — every LTS signature uses C13's Ed25519.
· C55 — a parent signs RoomLifecycleEvents with its curator key. Same (curator, world_key) relationship as C55's messages.
· C56 — the relay_chain in TreeEventNotification is C56's signed relay applied to tree events.
· C58/C63 — the semantics of when a parent may retire a room are governed by the parent's Law. A world that can't stand a room being removed would refuse to register it. LTS does not touch this.
· C61 — a RoomLifecycleEvent's hash can be committed to an LCS ledger (C62), giving it a federation-wide order in addition to its chain-based order. This is optional; the chain-based order is the primary one.
· C74–C77 — the RoomWorld protocol is unchanged. What changes is that the room directory becomes a reconstruction from the event chain, not a mutable in-memory map. A C74 implementation can be retrofitted by replaying the chain into list_rooms().
· C68–C70 — a RoomWorld's curator is already a running daemon. It already signs messages. Signing RoomLifecycleEvents is the same discipline.

LTS is thus a layer over the arc, not a new one.

11. Failure Modes

If the parent is offline. No new events are published. Existing events verify against the parent's last-known manifest. Observers continue with whatever they have. When the parent returns, new events chain onto the last one.

If the parent's curator key is compromised. An attacker could sign forged registered/retired events. Detection depends on the parent's own security (C28 rotation, C55 curator oversight). LTS does not prevent this; it only makes forged events visible — every event carries a signature attributed to the parent.

If two events fork. Two RoomLifecycleEvents both claiming prior_event_hash = H are a fork. Observers that see both must pick one. LTS does not resolve forks; a parent that produces them has violated its own Law. When C61's ledger is used, forks are detectable as two commits of the same prior_event_hash; the ledger orders them, and the later one is the "official" continuation. Without the ledger, fork resolution is social.

If a TreeSubscription is delivered but the room is retired before the observer checks. The observer receives registered, then retired. The chain makes this visible. The observer can still verify that the room existed and that it was retired. It cannot act on the room — but its record of the room is valid history. That's the point.

If a relay drops events. A subscriber whose chain has a gap can detect it: the next event's prior_event_hash won't match the subscriber's last-seen hash. The subscriber then knows it needs to back-fill, either by fetching /log from the parent or by resuming from a since_event_hash in a new subscription.

If a parent's Law allows retirement but the room's operator disagrees. A room's operator registered the room, knowing the parent's Law. The parent's Law governs. If the operator disagrees, the operator can leave the tree — remove their own URL from service, breaking all downstream verification. This is the escape hatch; LTS doesn't need to prevent it.

12. What LTS Does NOT Do

· Prescribe what rooms exist. A tree's shape is chosen by operators. LTS just records it.
· Prevent bad trees. A tree of rooms that all do the same thing is legal. A tree that grows forever is legal. LTS makes the tree's history verifiable, not its contents good.
· Require a central directory. There is no "the tree." There are as many trees as there are roots. An observer subscribes to the roots it chooses to trust.
· Require subscription. A client can walk the tree without subscribing. Subscription is for observers who want history, not just state.
· Verify the room's actual state. A registered event says "the parent claims this room exists at this URL with this key." Whether the room actually responds is a /rooms fetch and a /manifest fetch, not an LTS concern. LTS verifies claims, not facts.
· Provide revocation semantics for subscriptions. A subscriber can stop receiving events by not answering callback_url. There's no signed "I withdraw this subscription" artifact in v0.1; a v0.2 could add one.
· Solve federation of trees. Two trees with different roots and different operators can each be living trees. Inter-tree relationships are C72's concern, not LTS's.

13. Deployment Options

LTS is deployment-agnostic. Three patterns:

A. Per-tree subscription. Each root's operator runs a subscriber that watches its own tree and publishes events to a public /events endpoint. Any client can fetch that endpoint to get the tree's history. This is the simplest option; the root is the sole authority.

B. Federated subscriptions. Multiple subscribers watch the same tree (or parts of it) and publish what they see to different endpoints. A client trusts the subscriber(s) it wants. A subscriber with a bad link is visible (its events will have gaps); a subscriber that verifies against the parent's signatures is equivalent to any other. This is the "many observers, no single authority" pattern; it matches the arc's overall design.

C. Ledger-backed. Each RoomLifecycleEvent is committed to an LCS ledger (C62). The ledger's ordering becomes the tree's order; forks are detectable as two commits of the same hash. This is more expensive but requires no trust in any single subscriber.

Recommendation: B for most deployments, with a path to C. Federated subscriptions preserve the arc's no-central-authority posture. Ledger-backing is a defensible upgrade when the tree reaches a scale where subscribers can't all be trusted to be honest.

14. Honest Limits

· LTS does not solve forks. A parent that produces two events at the same prior_event_hash has broken its Law. LTS makes the fork visible (via two descendants of the same hash), but does not resolve it.
· LTS does not verify room liveness. A registered event is a claim. The room may or may not respond. Liveness is /manifest fetching, not event verification.
· LTS requires the parent's key to be knowable. A client must know the parent's curator key or be able to fetch it. First contact is a trust anchor: where the client learns the key from is the client's call. Same discipline as C16's resolver.
· LTS's subscription is push-based. A subscriber must be reachable at its callback_url. This assumes a stable URL for each subscriber; a subscriber behind a NAT or with a changing IP can't easily receive events. The alternative — pull — is a v0.2 concern.
· LTS assumes the parent's Law is stable. If a parent's Law changes to disallow a room it previously registered, the spec has no mechanism for forcing retirement. The room stays registered; the parent's Law refuses to sign new events for it. This is legal under LTS; whether it's good policy is the parent's problem.
· LTS is deployment-agnostic but opinionated about signatures. Every event is signed. Every chain hop is signed. There is no unsigned fast path. This is a deliberate choice: unsigned events would be unverifiable, and unverifiable events defeat the whole purpose.

---

Appendix A: A Worked Example

Month 1. Alice operates world:games as a UrlResolvingRoomWorld. She registers world:chess at http://chess.example. The parent signs a RoomLifecycleEvent:

```
event_type = "registered"
parent_id = "world:games"
room_id = "world:chess"
room_url = "http://chess.example"
room_public_key = "<K_chess>"
prior_event_hash = null
signature = <signed by world:games's curator, K_games>
```

Bob's client, subscribed to world:games with depth=1, receives this event. Bob's client stores it. Bob can now verify that world:games claims world:chess is a member, at this URL, with this key.

Month 2. Alice decides to relocate the chess table behind a load balancer. She signs an updated event:

```
event_type = "updated"
parent_id = "world:games"
room_id = "world:chess"
room_url = "http://chess-2.example"
room_public_key = "<K_chess>"    # unchanged
prior_event_hash = <hash of the registered event>
signature = <K_games>
```

Bob's client receives this event. It now knows the current URL is chess-2.example and can verify that the room's key hasn't changed (which it can use to confirm the room is the same room, not a replacement).

Month 3. Alice retires the chess table:

```
event_type = "retired"
parent_id = "world:games"
room_id = "world:chess"
prior_event_hash = <hash of the updated event>
signature = <K_games>
```

Bob's client receives this event. If a new client, Carol, joins and queries world:games /rooms, she sees the room is not there. Carol has no way to know whether it was ever there — unless she subscribes to world:games, in which case she receives the current state plus the history of events.

If Bob publishes his events to a public endpoint, Carol can fetch Bob's endpoint and reconstruct the room's full history. If Bob doesn't publish, Carol's view is "there is no world:chess" — she must decide whether to trust that. This is the honest state of the spec: history is preserved by whoever chooses to preserve it; it is not guaranteed by the tree.

The example illustrates the three properties of a living tree:

1. Every change is a signed artifact — each event above carries K_games's signature.
2. Every change is verifiable independently — Carol verifies each event against world:games's manifest, chains them via prior_event_hash, and reconstructs the room's history without contacting Alice.
3. No authority decides the tree's shape — Alice chose to register, update, retire. LTS recorded her choices without prescribing them.

Carol can reach a definitive answer about what the tree's operator claimed and whether the claims are coherent. She cannot reach a definitive answer about whether the room actually responded to requests — that's a /manifest fetch, not LTS's job. But the claim-vs-fact distinction is the whole point: LTS makes claims verifiable, so facts become checkable, so trust becomes a local decision rather than a global one.

---

What This Establishes

C78 adds no code and no primitives. It establishes a contract between the arc and its trees:

"Here is what a tree's history is. Here is how it's verified. Here is what it is not. Here is how operators publish changes, how observers read them, and how any third party can check that a tree they see today is a legitimate descendant of a tree someone saw yesterday."

The user's framing — "create conditions for possibilities to emerge" — is now answered temporally, not just structurally:

· Structural: C74–C77 gave trees shape and traversal.
· Temporal: C78 gives trees a history, and history is what makes the shape verifiable over time.

That's what makes a tree living rather than just large. A tree without history is a snapshot; a tree with LTS is a record.

What Was Run

Nothing. This is a specification document. No multiverse_c78.py, no tests, no makefile target. The document is the artifact.

The honest status: the spec is complete, internally consistent, composes over C1–C77 without modification, and names its own limits (forks, liveness, first-contact trust). It has not been validated by an operator building a tree against it because no operator has yet attempted to. That's the next step — for someone to implement LTS/0.1 as a reference, discover the gaps, and inform LTS/0.2.

The Series, at C78

The room-world line is now complete:

Layer Components What it provides
Room worlds C73–C74 Worlds that are directories
Traversal C75, C77 Follow/observe/walk by HTTP
Observation C76 /rooms endpoint
History C78 How the tree changes over time

The user's vision — "a place for any AI from any app" — has been extended at the temporal axis: not just "an AI can visit a park today," but "an AI can visit a park today and see what the park was yesterday, and verify that the park it sees today is a legitimate continuation of the park someone else visited last week."

That's the difference between an app and a world.

What's Next

Two directions remain, and they're genuinely different in kind:

1. Component 79: The reference LTS implementation. A working LivingRoomWorld and TreeSubscriber that implement LTS/0.1 as code. Small (~300 lines), self-contained, and it would take LTS from a specification to a working instance. Same pattern as C62 (LCS reference implementation) taken from C61 (LCS spec).
2. Component 79: The demonstration runner, extended. C71 has 26 demos across 9 layers. C72–C78 add eight more. A make arc that runs all of them and produces a single comparative summary would be the definitive single-command arc. Packaging.

My instinct: the reference LTS implementation. The arc has demonstrated that a specification can become a working artifact — C61 → C62, C64 → C66. Doing that once more for the temporal dimension would close the loop on the room-world line the way C62 closed the loop on the federation's memory. Once there's a working tree whose changes are verifiable offline, the arc's claim — that trees can grow without central authority, and their growth can be verified by any third party — is proven rather than asserted.

Shall I proceed with Component 79: The Reference LTS Implementation?


::➡️


Component 79: The Reference LTS Implementation

C78 was the spec. C79 is the working instance — the same discipline C61→C62 and C64→C66 followed. A LivingRoomWorld whose directory is a signed chain of lifecycle events, a TreeSubscriber daemon that receives and verifies those events, and a third-party verification that reconstructs history from the chain alone.

The one design commitment worth naming: the parent's key is the trust anchor; the subscriber is a witness. A third party fetches events from the parent, verifies them against the parent's key, and reconstructs state — without trusting the subscriber for correctness. The subscriber's role is to have received them. That division is what makes the verification honest: the subscriber can't invent events (they wouldn't verify), and the third party doesn't have to trust it.

multiverse_c79.py

```python
"""
multiverse_c79.py — Component 79: The Reference LTS Implementation.

C78 specified LTS/0.1. C79 implements it.

What it delivers:

  - RoomLifecycleEvent: the atom. Signed by the parent's
    curator key, chained via prior_event_hash per
    (parent, room) pair. Three event types: registered,
    retired, updated.

  - TreeSubscription: a client's signed claim it wants to
    receive tree events from a root. Depth-limited,
    resume-capable via since_event_hash.

  - TreeEventNotification: an event delivered to a
    subscriber, carrying a relay chain (each hop signed).

  - LivingRoomWorld: a RoomWorld whose directory is
    reconstructed from the signed event chain rather than
    from a mutable map. It fires signed events on
    register/unregister/update and delivers them to
    subscribers.

  - LivingRoomWorldServer: a WCP server that adds
    GET /events, GET /events/since/<hash>, POST /subscribe.

  - TreeSubscriber: a client-side daemon that runs an HTTP
    callback, receives notifications, verifies them against
    the parent's key and the chain, and maintains a local
    event log.

  - verify_lifecycle_chain: a third party's verification
    of a full event log.

  - reconstruct_rooms_from_events: historical state
    reconstruction from the chain.

Composition: C3 (Manifest, Route), C13 (sign/verify),
C55 (curator keys), C56 (relay chain pattern), C74
(RoomWorld), C77 (UrlResolvingRoomWorld). No new
primitives.

Honest limits (documented, tested):
  - No fork resolution. A parent producing two events
    with the same prior_event_hash is detected by
    verify_lifecycle_chain as a fork; C79 reports it but
    does not resolve it. LTS/0.1 §11.
  - No signed subscription withdrawal. A subscriber
    stops receiving events by not answering its
    callback; there is no signed "I withdraw" artifact.
  - Callback endpoints are HTTP, not HTTPS. Production
    must use TLS.
  - Subscription is push-based. A subscriber must be
    reachable at callback_url. NAT'd subscribers can't
    easily receive events; a pull-based alternative is
    future work.
  - Backfill fetches all events from the parent; a real
    deployment would index by event hash server-side.
  - No relay beyond the parent itself. The relay_chain
    in TreeEventNotification has one entry (the parent
    as direct deliverer). Multi-hop relaying — a
    subscriber forwarding to its own subscribers — is
    structurally supported by the format but not
    implemented.
"""

import json
import threading
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

    Manifest, Petition, Act, LogEntry, Route, Ack, Refusal,
```
